mainEntity.name: Is it normal for a new veneer to feel slightly rough at first?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is not uncommon for a new veneer to feel slightly unfamiliar or subtly different when you first run your tongue across it. During the placement appointment, your dentist will adjust and polish the veneer, but occasionally minor irregularities may remain. These can often be resolved with a brief follow-up appointment for additional polishing. If the roughness is sharp, uncomfortable, or does not improve within a few days, it is advisable to contact your dental practice so they can assess and smooth the surface as needed.

mainEntity.name: Can a rough veneer damage my tongue?

acceptedAnswer.text: A sharply chipped veneer edge can occasionally cause minor irritation to the tongue or inner lip if the edge is sufficiently sharp. In most cases, this is not a serious concern, but it is uncomfortable and worth having addressed promptly. Your dentist can smooth or polish a rough or sharp edge, often in a brief appointment. If you are experiencing persistent tongue irritation alongside the rough sensation, do arrange an assessment sooner rather than later to prevent ongoing discomfort.

mainEntity.name: How long should veneers last before they start to show signs of wear?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of a veneer depends on the material used, the individual patient's bite and habits, and the quality of ongoing maintenance. Porcelain veneers, with appropriate care, may last many years. Longevity varies considerably between individuals depending on clinical factors, habits, and maintenance, and your dentist can advise you on what to expect in your specific circumstances. Composite veneers typically have a shorter lifespan and may require more frequent repair or replacement. Regular dental reviews allow your dentist to monitor your veneers and advise you in a timely manner if any intervention would be beneficial.

mainEntity.name: Can a veneer that feels rough be repaired without full replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes. If the roughness is due to surface wear, the veneer may be polished to restore a smoother finish. Small chips along the edge of a composite veneer can often be repaired with additional composite material. Porcelain veneers that have minor chip damage may also be smoothed in some cases, though larger fractures may necessitate replacement. Whether repair or replacement is appropriate depends entirely on the specific clinical situation, which your dentist will assess during examination.

mainEntity.name: Does a rough veneer margin mean decay is developing underneath?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rough or open margin does not automatically mean that decay is present, but it does create a surface area where plaque and bacteria can accumulate more easily. If this area is not kept clean, there is a risk over time that decay could develop at the tooth-veneer junction. This is one of the reasons why margin changes should be assessed promptly by a dentist rather than monitored indefinitely at home. Radiographs may be taken to evaluate the underlying tooth if there is any clinical concern.

mainEntity.name: Should I stop brushing the area if my veneer feels rough?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It is important to continue brushing and flossing the area, as allowing plaque to build up around a veneer margin can compound any existing concerns. Use a soft-bristled toothbrush and gentle technique rather than avoiding the area entirely. If the roughness is causing significant discomfort during brushing, contact your dental practice to arrange a timely assessment, and your dentist can advise you on the most appropriate way to maintain hygiene in that area while awaiting your appointment.
